body.en: A differential equation relates a function to its own rate of change — and rates of change are how most of the physical world is actually described: a population's growth rate depends on its current size, a cooling object's temperature falls at a rate proportional to how far above room temperature it still is, a radioactive sample decays at a rate proportional to how much is left. Calculus gave you derivatives; this chapter is about running that machinery in reverse — starting from a stated relationship between a function and its derivative, and recovering the function itself.

A differential equation is an equation relating an unknown function \( y=y(x) \) to one or more of its derivatives. The order of the equation is the order of the highest derivative that appears; this chapter deals only with first-order equations, involving \( y' \) but no higher derivative.

A solution on an interval \( I \) is a differentiable function \( y(x) \) that satisfies the equation for every \( x\in I \). The general solution is the whole family of solutions, typically written with one arbitrary constant \( C \); if a condition \( y(x_0)=y_0 \) is also specified, the problem is called an initial value problem (IVP) — it asks for a solution passing through that point. An IVP doesn't automatically pick out a unique member of the general solution's family: existence and uniqueness require additional hypotheses, which this chapter's examples all happen to satisfy but which aren't checked here in general. When a solution to an IVP is found, it's called a particular solution.

Verify that \( y=Ce^{2x} \) is a solution of \( \dfrac{dy}{dx}=2y \) for any constant \( C \), show that these are the only solutions, then find the particular solution satisfying \( y(0)=5 \).

These are solutions: differentiating, \( \dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{d}{dx}\big[Ce^{2x}\big]=2Ce^{2x}=2\big(Ce^{2x}\big)=2y \) — the equation holds for every \( C \).

These are the only solutions: if \( y \) is any solution of \( y'=2y \), then \[ \frac{d}{dx}\big[e^{-2x}y\big]=e^{-2x}\big(y'-2y\big)=e^{-2x}(0)=0, \] so \( e^{-2x}y \) is constant on the interval — call it \( C \) — meaning \( y=Ce^{2x} \) after all. So \( y=Ce^{2x} \) is genuinely the general solution, not just a family of solutions.

Applying the initial condition: \( y(0)=Ce^{0}=C=5 \), so the particular solution is \( y=5e^{2x} \).

A first-order equation is separable if it can be written in the form \[ \frac{dy}{dx}=f(x)\,g(y), \] where the right-hand side factors into a function of \( x \) alone times a function of \( y \) alone. Every example in this chapter is separable — it's the first and most widely applicable technique for solving a differential equation in closed form.

value.en: Before dividing by \( g(y) \), find its zeros: every constant \( a \) with \( g(a)=0 \) gives a constant solution \( y(x)=a \), which the division in the next step would otherwise silently lose
\( \displaystyle\int\frac{1}{g(y)}\,dy=\int f(x)\,dx+C \) — one arbitrary constant is enough, since combining both sides' constants just renames it

An implicit relation between \( x \) and \( y \) already counts as a solution just as validly as an explicit \( y(x) \) — the remaining work is identifying a differentiable branch of it, and the interval on which the original equation actually makes sense

label.en: ▲ Theorem 1.1 — Separation on a nonzero branch

body.en: Let \( I \) and \( J \) be open intervals. Suppose \( f \) is continuous on \( I \), and \( g \) is continuous and nonzero on \( J \). Let \( F \) be an antiderivative of \( f \) on \( I \), and \( G \) an antiderivative of \( \dfrac{1}{g} \) on \( J \) (so \( G'(y)=\dfrac{1}{g(y)} \) for \( y\in J \)). Then a differentiable function \( y:I\to J \) solves \[ \frac{dy}{dx}=f(x)\,g(y) \] if and only if \[ G(y(x))=F(x)+C \] for some constant \( C \). (Since \( g \) is nonzero throughout \( J \) by assumption, this covers every solution staying on one nonzero branch of \( g \) — a constant solution sitting at a zero of \( g \) is a separate case, found directly rather than through this formula.)

(⇒) Suppose \( y(x) \) solves the equation, with \( g(y(x))\neq0 \). Dividing both sides by \( g(y(x)) \): \[ \frac{1}{g(y(x))}\,y'(x)=f(x). \] By the chain rule, \( \dfrac{d}{dx}\big[G(y(x))\big]=G'(y(x))\,y'(x)=\dfrac{1}{g(y(x))}\,y'(x) \), so the left side above is exactly \( \dfrac{d}{dx}\big[G(y(x))\big] \), and the equation becomes \[ \frac{d}{dx}\big[G(y(x))\big]=f(x)=\frac{d}{dx}\big[F(x)\big]. \] So \( G(y(x))-F(x) \) has zero derivative on the interval, hence is a constant \( C \): \( G(y(x))=F(x)+C \).

(⇐) Conversely, suppose \( G(y(x))=F(x)+C \). Differentiating both sides with respect to \( x \) (chain rule on the left): \[ G'(y(x))\,y'(x)=F'(x) \;\Longrightarrow\; \frac{1}{g(y(x))}\,y'(x)=f(x). \] Since \( g(y(x))\neq0 \) by hypothesis, multiplying both sides by \( g(y(x)) \) gives \( y'(x)=f(x)\,g(y(x)) \) — exactly the original equation.

label.en: Worked example 1.B — Solving an initial value problem

body.en:
Solve \( \dfrac{dy}{dx}=xy \), \( y(0)=3 \).

First, the equilibrium: \( g(y)=y \) has the single zero \( y=0 \), giving the constant solution \( y\equiv0 \) (indeed \( \frac{d}{dx}[0]=0=x\cdot0 \)).

For \( y\neq0 \), separate: \[ \frac{dy}{y}=x\,dx. \] Integrate both sides: \[ \ln|y|=\frac{x^2}{2}+C. \] Exponentiate: \( |y|=e^{x^2/2+C}=e^{C}e^{x^2/2} \); writing \( A=\pm e^{C} \) (necessarily nonzero, since \( e^{C}>0 \)) absorbs the sign, giving the nonzero-branch family \( y=Ae^{x^2/2} \), \( A\neq0 \). Combined with the equilibrium above — exactly this formula's \( A=0 \) case — the complete general solution is \[ y=Ae^{x^2/2},\qquad A\in\mathbb{R}. \] Applying \( y(0)=3 \): \( A\cdot e^{0}=A=3 \). So \[ y=3e^{x^2/2}. \]

A radioactive sample decays at a rate proportional to the amount present: \( \dfrac{dN}{dt}=-kN \) for a constant \( k>0 \), with \( N(0)=N_0 \) and \( N_0>0 \). Find \( N(t) \), and express the half-life \( T \) (the time at which \( N=N_0/2 \)) in terms of \( k \).

Separate: \( \dfrac{dN}{N}=-k\,dt \) (valid since \( N>0 \)), so \( \ln N=-kt+C \), giving \( N=Ae^{-kt} \); \( N(0)=A=N_0 \), so \[ N(t)=N_0e^{-kt}. \] Setting \( N(T)=N_0/2 \): \( e^{-kT}=\tfrac12 \), so \( -kT=-\ln2 \), and \[ T=\frac{\ln2}{k}. \] The half-life doesn't depend on \( N_0 \) — a hallmark of exponential decay (the assumption \( N_0>0 \) matters: if \( N_0=0 \) the sample is identically zero, and "half of nothing" isn't a meaningful time to solve for) — and the same reasoning (with \( k<0 \) reinterpreted as growth) drives unconstrained population-growth models.

Every example above reduced to the same moves: check for equilibrium solutions, separate, integrate, solve for \( y \) (or accept an implicit relation when that last step isn't possible in closed form). Not every first-order equation is separable — the next stage of this track extends the method to equations that aren't, starting with linear first-order equations and the integrating-factor technique.
